channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You eventually trust a source you once thought was lying.
item.description: A 1951 study found that persuasive messages from unreliable sources become more convincing over time.

item.title: You find it impossible to remember what it is like to be ignorant.
item.description: A 1989 study found that better-informed agents cannot accurately anticipate the judgments and market valuations of less-informed agents.

item.title: You retroactively invent reasons to prefer your choice.
item.description: A 2007 study found that people misremember the features of rejected options to make their chosen one seem superior.

item.title: You like people just because you see them often.
item.description: A 1950 study found that physical proximity is a significant predictor of friendship formation, working in tandem with similarity.

item.title: You are convinced you are a better driver than most.
item.description: A 1981 study of student participants found that 93% of the U.S. sample rated their driving skills as being in the top 50%.

item.title: You believe that luck is a balancing force.
item.description: A 1971 study by Tversky and Kahneman, titled 'Belief in the Law of Small Numbers,' found that people expect short-term streaks of randomness to correct themselves, even when the odds never change.

item.title: Bad news is heavier than good news.
item.description: A 2008 review found that humans process negative stimuli faster, remember them longer, and react to them more intensely.

item.title: You think your virtues are unique, but your vices are normal.
item.description: The 1987 study by Suls and Wan demonstrated that people tend to underestimate the commonality of their positive or healthy traits (the False Uniqueness Effect).

item.title: You expect your future self to work perfectly.
item.description: A 1994 study found that people consistently underestimate how long tasks take, even when they know their own history of being late.

item.title: Your initial estimate is a trap you set.
item.description: A 1974 study showed that people's final estimates for unknown quantities are heavily skewed by the first arbitrary number they hear.

item.title: Fear and attraction often feel exactly the same.
item.description: A 1974 study found that men were significantly more likely to call a female interviewer after crossing a scary suspension bridge.

item.title: Your memory of an event is not a summary.
item.description: A 1993 study proposed that people disproportionately weight peak intensity and the final moment when evaluating experiences, though research indicates duration remains a significant factor in overall evaluation.

item.title: A rumor becomes truth if it is repeated enough.
item.description: The availability cascade is a self-reinforcing process in which an idea gains social momentum through the interaction of the availability heuristic and reputational incentives.

item.title: You miss the obvious when your focus is occupied.
item.description: Participants often fail to notice a prominent stimulus, like a person in a costume, when they are engaged in a simple counting task.

item.title: You fear risk more when the outlook is positive.
item.description: People show a strong preference for certainty when a positive outcome is likely, even when a riskier option offers a higher expected value.

item.title: You overestimate your ability on tasks you find difficult.
item.description: The hard-easy effect describes the tendency to overestimate one's own performance on hard tasks and underestimate it on easy ones.

item.title: Your mood depends entirely on what you track.
item.description: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are currently thinking about it.

item.title: You accept the status quo because it was chosen.
item.description: When presented with a default option, individuals are significantly more likely to stick with it than to choose an alternative.

item.title: You value your possessions more than they are worth.
item.description: People demand a higher price to sell an item they own than they would pay to acquire that exact same item.

item.title: You believe you have finally finished changing your personality.
item.description: In a 2013 study of 7,500 adults, participants consistently underestimated how much their personality, values, and preferences would continue to shift over the next decade.

item.title: Your sense of self-worth is tethered to others' success.
item.description: Individuals prefer to evaluate their abilities using objective standards when available, turning to social comparison only when such objective means are lacking.

item.title: Your judgment of quality is anchored to recent experience.
item.description: The contrast effect is a established psychological phenomenon where perceptions are influenced by preceding, contrasting stimuli.

item.title: You ignore the statistics to focus on the story.
item.description: People disregard general statistical information in favor of specific, anecdotal evidence.

item.title: Your brain gives more weight to bad news.
item.description: While Hansen and Hansen (1988) identified an 'anger superiority effect,' subsequent research indicates this finding is likely an artifact of low-level visual features in the stimuli rather than an innate psychological bias toward negative information.

item.title: Nothing is as important as you think it is.
item.description: People misjudge the long-term impact of life events because they focus too heavily on them at the moment.

item.title: You assume your opinions are more common than they are.
item.description: People consistently overestimate the extent to which others share their own beliefs.

item.title: The pain of losing is stronger than the joy of winning.
item.description: Prospect theory demonstrates that losses are weighted more heavily than equivalent gains, a phenomenon known as loss aversion.

item.title: You are more likeable when you make a mistake.
item.description: Competent individuals who commit a small, embarrassing blunder are rated as more attractive than those who remain perfect.

item.title: You judge your future self by your current needs.
item.description: Projection bias causes people to overestimate the degree to which their future tastes and preferences will resemble their current ones.

item.title: You struggle to solve problems you have used before.
item.description: Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias where you become unable to see an object as having any function other than its original one.

item.title: You conform to the group to avoid social discomfort.
item.description: A majority of participants conformed to an obviously incorrect group consensus on at least one occasion, though most individual responses remained correct.

item.title: You try to suppress thoughts and make them louder.
item.description: The 'ironic process theory' suggests that the effort to suppress a specific thought makes it more cognitively accessible.

item.title: You treat the same amount of money differently.
item.description: Mental accounting causes people to categorize money into different 'accounts' based on the source, leading to irrational spending.

item.title: You interpret luck as evidence of your own skill.
item.description: People who perceive a sense of control over a random event significantly overestimate their probability of success.

item.title: You are harder on yourself during simple tasks.
item.description: Social facilitation reveals that the presence of others improves performance on simple, well-rehearsed tasks but degrades performance on complex ones.

item.title: You assume people notice your mood more than they do.
item.description: The 'illusion of transparency' causes individuals to overestimate how much their internal state is visible to others.

item.title: Your confidence in a decision increases after you act.
item.description: Post-decision dissonance reduction causes people to rate their chosen option as significantly better than an rejected alternative immediately after making the choice.

item.title: You attribute your own poor choices to the situation.
item.description: This phenomenon is known as the actor-observer bias, not the fundamental attribution error.

item.title: You take the credit and blame the world.
item.description: A 1975 study by Miller and Ross examined the self-serving bias, questioning whether the attribution of success to internal factors and failure to external ones is a defense mechanism or a byproduct of information processing.

item.title: You will change your answer to fit the group.
item.description: A 1951 study found that 74% of participants gave at least one incorrect answer to a simple task to match the majority.

item.title: You adopt the mood of the room without choosing.
item.description: A 1994 research review found that people automatically mimic the facial expressions and postures of those around them.

item.title: One positive trait blinds you to every other defect.
item.description: A 1920 study found that officers who rated a soldier highly in one category consistently rated them highly in all unrelated categories.

item.title: You exert less effort when you are not alone.
item.description: A 1913 study found that individuals pulling on a rope in a group exert less force than when pulling individually.

item.title: The more you try not to think, the more.
item.description: A 1994 study revealed that instructions to suppress a specific thought result in that thought becoming more cognitively accessible.

item.title: You judge others by their character, not their context.
item.description: A 1967 study found that people attributed views expressed in an essay to the writer's internal beliefs, even when told the writer had no choice in the topic.

item.title: A repeated claim eventually feels like a known truth.
item.description: A 2015 study found that even clearly false headlines are rated as more accurate simply because they have been seen before.

item.title: You believe the world is fundamentally fair to everyone.
item.description: A 1966 study demonstrated that people will blame victims for their own misfortune to maintain the belief that people generally get what they deserve.

item.title: You mistake your own point of view for objective reality.
item.description: Research indicates that people assume their view of the world is based on unbiased information, while those who disagree with them are biased by their ideology.

item.title: You continue losing ventures because of the investment already made.
item.description: A 1985 study found that people are more likely to continue investing in a failing project if they have already committed significant time or money to it.

item.title: A small favor makes a large request more likely.
item.description: A 1966 study found that people who agreed to a trivial request were significantly more likely to agree to a larger, related request a few days later.
